The first phase consists of an assessment of drone ecosystems in the region along with international best experiences and a thorough market analysis for drone services in the whole LAC region as well as in selected international benchmark countries.
The report gives an overview of the current state and maturity level of drone ecosystems in the LAC region as well as evaluates the adoption level of key drone use cases.

Additionally, it showcases an analysis of global regulatory and UTM trends, international UAS ecosystem benchmarks from 5 countries (USA, Switzerland, Poland, Spain and Rwanda), and a detailed look into selected LAC countries.
The report presents a market analysis, calculating the current and forecasted market potential for drone services in different industries until 2026 per country.
The report showcases the job creation potential of the UAS commercial service industry, as well as the number of commercial and recreational drones forecasted until 2026.

The second phase is focused on use cases for drone technology in development activities in the LAC region along with the business models and strategic drone development initiatives that were created as a result of an in-depth analysis of global best practices and local requirements.
The report showcases the analysis of the potential of the adoption of drone technologies for development.
The broad study covers 14 use cases, including the SDGs impacted, relevant social and environmental challenges that drones can solve, and proposed pilot projects.
Furthermore, adoption enablers and barriers along with business models are described in detail.

The report covers the identification of key initiatives that are necessary to ensure the expansion and consolidation of the drone ecosystem for the next five years in order to unlock the potential of the lower skies in the LAC region.
Two illustrative development roadmaps for early stage and intermediate/advanced drone ecosystems are provided.
The third phase is based on a deep-dive into Guatemala, Brazil (Tocantins State), and Haiti as some prevalent case-studies of the LAC region.
In addition to country reports, snapshots and executive summaries of reports from Phases I and II were developed.

The Latin American and the Caribbean region is rich in culture and biodiversity, and includes some of the most rapidly-developing economies in the world, and yet experiences some of the highest rates of inequality in the world.

This report identifies critical sectors and areas where the use of drone technology can substantially support to address important social and environmental challenges faced by countries in the region.
These issues are associated with the geographical location, rapid urban sprawling, isolation and lack of development in rural areas.

At the same time, there are important demographic differences and diversification in economic advancement between countries, combined with rapid and unequal regional, national and local transformations.
In this context looking for long-lasting and innovative solutions is becoming increasingly important, where drones can take a critical role.

Hence, to unlock regional potential and ensure proper wellbeing of its citizens, 14 development drone use cases were identified for the region: healthcare, agriculture, humanitarian aid, disaster management, urban planning and monitoring, road infrastructure maintenance, restoration and reforestation, road traffic and safety monitoring, remote internet access, endangered species monitoring, wildfires, fighting with mosquito-borne diseases, environmental pollution monitoring, waste management and landfill monitoring.

The broad analysis of the drone applications for each of the use cases results in detailed description and deep understanding of the potential and requirements for the implementation of drone technology in development activities.
Multiple aspects were taken into consideration such as maturity of the drone applications, benefits that drones can bring to the region or expected outcomes and impact of their use.
The report identifies enabling factors, both technological and regulatory of the drone solution implementation and lists the adoption enablers and barriers.

Removing barriers to drone adoption requires commitment from public and private sectors, the support of NGOs and international financial organisations, along with awareness and participation from civil society and communities.
That is why, for each use case, the list of relevant stakeholders is proposed.
Several potential business models for drone deployment in the LCR region are suggested, dependent on requirements like scale and frequency of operations, and various possible sources of funding.
Finally, to facilitate introduction and scale-up of the use of drones in the region, an exemplary plan for drone pilot project implementation and a “success story” from the region is presented.

The operating model for drone applications is usually either ‘in-house’, where operations are conducted using an institution’s internal capacity, or outsourced, where responsibility is given to a third-party drone service provider.

In-house models can potentially offer greater flexibility and faster response time, but will require significant investment in terms of technology, staff, and other capabilities, with associated financial risk.
Outsourcing drastically reduces these initial costs and risks, as well as simplifying issues of compliance and permits, but can lead to inflexibility and a lack of agility.
Other, less common operating models embrace the sharing economy and the idea of ‘collaborative consumption’.

In a co-operative or community-run drone project, a community (for example, a group of farmers) might purchase a drone, sharing the cost of the equipment and its maintenance, giving them all access to the technology.
Alternatively, ‘ drone sharing’ can connect individual end-users and drone owners, potentially using an online platform to create connections within the drone community.
These models are usually appropriate only for small-scale, local projects.

build-operate-transfer (BOT) model: Generally, this model is used in public sector organisations, where a third-party company or consultant is responsible for establishing and running the organisation, building the team etc., and gradually transfers the knowledge in house over time.
When the public sector organisation has gained enough experience and has the appropriate staff to manage operations itself, the consultant withdraws.
The choice of model is likely to depend on a number of factors defining the nature of the project, including scale and regularity.

For instance, operations may be planned on a local, regional, or nationwide scale, while deployment may be ad-hoc (in response to emergencies like natural disasters and wildfires), regular (for cyclical monitoring of urban planning or wildlife), or permanent (e.g., agricultural monitoring or long-term medical delivery system).

In 2019, WeRobotics and Flying Labs conducted a drone delivery pilot project in the Dominican Republic.
The project was funded by Pfizer and focused on using affordable, locally repairable and locally owned cargo drones to deliver essential medicines to remote health facilities .

Dominican Republic Flying Labs is a local knowledge hub that focuses on the use of drones, robotics, data, and AI for positive social change, and WeRobotics is a non-profit organisation that uses drones for humanitarian purposes.
Local communities in the remote mountains of the Dominican Republic do not have regular access to healthcare services.
The challenge here is the cost of local transportation and a limited number of local transportation options, rather than scarcity of proper infrastructure.
When local clinics run out of medicines, or when they cannot test patient samples locally, patients have to travel to the hospital in person.
Even if the patient can afford it, getting to the hospital may require a full day of travel.
Taking a full day away from paid work or family responsibilities is often not an option.
Some patients are too frail to travel on the back of motorbikes on bumpy and windy roads.
In many cases, local medical staff have to organise transportation of samples or medical goods using their personal transportation resources, as there is no other option for helping patients.
Flying Labs pilots trained by WeRobotics carried out six weeks of consecutive deliveries in the province of San Juan de la Maguana between June and July 2019.
A total of 101 autonomous flights were carried out from Bohechio Hospital to two separate health facilities, traveling a total of 994 kilometres .
Of the 51 outbound flights, 40 carried medicines totalling 21.25 kilos.
The altitude difference between the two locations was 784 meters.
During the project, flights were conducted under various weather conditions and operational scenarios, and all of the deliveries were successful, with no major incidents reported.

The analysis of the results of the pilot project showed that the cost of delivery was approximately $0.40 per km for 5 flights per day with drones, compared to $0.43 per km for land transport (a 7% cost savings per km).
Further cost savings may be achieved if the number of flights per day increases from 5 to 8, resulting in 23% cost savings per km (($0.33/km drone vs. $0.43/km land).
With 26 flights per day, cost per km decreases further to $0.25/km by drone, which represents a cost saving of 42%.

Drones are becoming an inseparable element of precision farming, helping agriculture professionals lead the way with sustainable farming practices while protecting production and increasing profitability.
Farmers deploy drones for mapping, crop fertilisation, seeding, soil quality analysis and harvest estimation.
Advanced sensors allow farmers to generate digital maps , showing insights impossible to see with the naked eye.

This use case is primarily related to precise, cyclical mapping of vegetation health, soil moisture, and fertilising requirements, with multispectral cameras being used to generate a map of vegetation indexes such as NDVI (Normalized difference vegetation index).
When adequately interpreted over time, autonomous farming equipment can use such maps to target specific plants with fertilizers, for example.
Drones enable the real-time and precise analysis of overall soil health: soil quality, nutrient management, and dead soil zones .
These factors influence farm productivity, and up-to-date data supports farmers in determining the most effective patterns for planting and managing crops.
Moreover, drones are used as a vehicle to perform crop spraying, especially in challenging terrain conditions.
Drones can increase spray speed fivefold compared to other types of machinery.
The advanced systems enable the volume of fertilizer applied to be optimised for the benefit of the natural environment.
In many cases, drones can also reduce the exposure of humans to chemicals.
Based on drone data, AI-augmented software can evaluate an approximate yield, e.g. amount of fruit.
Based on this information, farmers can make logistic decisions and optimize field management.
Finally, drones can be used for disaster (e.g. flood) prediction, to warn farmers of potential threats.
Since the birth of precision farming in the mid-90s, drones have become an integral part of agriculture development.
Nowadays, the agriculture sector around the globe actively deploys drone technologies.

LAC countries have been early adopters of agriculture drones, with Guatemala starting commercial drone operations in 2012.
The technology is especially well-established in crop spraying, where it has been present for at least a decade in Guatemala, Brazil and Argentina .

There are 300,000 small farming families in El Salvador, whose crops (and therefore livelihoods and diets) are at the mercy of pests and extreme weather events .

These are issues they have in common with many other farming communities worldwide: There are 30,000 types of weed, 10,000 varieties of insect, and 3,000 different fungal pathogens that threaten food crops around the world.
For a subsistence farmer, the threat is even more profound.
Most obviously, a precarious financial situation reduces their purchasing ability, but in addition, they face limited access to technology, information, markets and services.
A farmer in El Salvador with just three hectares of land will earn less than $130 per month, and a pest outbreak could potentially reduce a family to destitution in a single season.

Farmers are always looking for ways to gain the upper hand in this battle—and drone technology has the potential to address the inequality of information and access, to help farmers protect their crops, improve yields , and thereby achieve greater profitability.
Chemicals have for many years been vital in helping farmers protect harvests and livelihoods, and estimates suggest that up to 60% of global crops are saved each year with the use of pesticides.
In developing countries, they often rely on backpack sprayers for the application of pesticides.
Drones can provide application up to 50 times faster than a typical backpack sprayer, reducing time spent on spraying—and even more significantly, reducing human exposure to chemicals.
Drones can use as little as 10% of the water compared to backpack sprayers, helping farmers conserve vital resources (particularly relevant in drought-prone areas).
The greater accuracy provided by drones also ensures less waste, and less danger of unintended environmental impact through runoff.
Effective crop protection fundamentally depends on farmers knowing how to treat their plants (and when), as well as being able to afford and accurately apply the treatment.
Drones help to identify pest threats more effectively than manual / human surveillance.
Early warning of pest activity gives farmers a head start, and a chance to save more of their crops.
With the use of data, drones are also able to deliver targeted chemical treatment, at the optimum place and time to protect crops.
This reduces the cost of treatment, as well as offering the potential for higher yields.
This doesn’t just affect farmers’ incomes, but results in increased food security in many developing countries—for example El Salvador, where 9% of the population is currently undernourished.

According to the World Bank, natural disasters in Latin America and the Caribbean push between 150,000 and 2.1 million people annually into extreme poverty.
Estimates for 2030 show even higher impacts on poverty, livelihoods and critical sectors of the economy.

The World Risk Index (2020) shows that over 50% of LAC countries are ranked high or very high for natural disaster occurrence, and are currently presenting high or very high levels of vulnerability to these hazards—including susceptibility, adaptability, and ability to cope with these events.

Hence, risk mitigation and planning activities, to ensure that countries are well-equipped to deal with these challenges, are critical in guaranteeing the safety and livelihoods of millions in the LAC region.
Between 2000 and 2019 alone, 152 million people in the region have been severely affected by a total of 1,205 disasters .
Earthquakes, floods, and storms are the natural events associated with the highest levels of deaths, affected populations, and economic losses.
Floods are the most common disaster in the LAC region, with 548 floods occurring since 2000.
Despite the relatively low death toll directly associated with floods, they have affected almost 41 million people and caused around US$26 billion in total damages.

Floods are one of the costliest natural disasters because of the damage caused—from impact on physical and environmental assets (including human belongings and shelter, ecological systems and production across economic sectors) to health-related issues and human deaths.
New methodologies and innovative technologies are required to complement the traditional approach to improve disaster management efficiency.
It is necessary to build an adequate system that incorporates telecommunication capabilities, remote sensing, and spatial and temporal oriented databases to store the vast amount of data.
Latin America and the Caribbean is the second-most disaster prone region in the world.
Countries in the LAC region are vulnerable to floods, tropical storms and hurricanes, earthquakes and tsunamis, droughts, landslides, extreme temperatures, volcanic events, wildfires , and more.
All natural disasters disrupt and endanger the normal functionality of communities, sometimes having extremely serious consequences on people, property, economies, and the environment.

Poor disaster management and/or planning—for example bad levee systems, insufficient shelters, lack of education & training, or any other shortcomings in preparation—can potentially worsen the outcomes of a disaster.
Overview of drone disaster management Disaster mitigation and preparedness: Key pre-disaster use cases include mitigation-related vulnerability assessments and risk modelling.
Drones can map and monitor the topography and surface features of areas susceptible to and impacted by fires, storms, landslides, earthquakes, or floods.
High-resolution drone imagery allows the creation of orthophotos and 3D models, which are further used for risk modelling of such disasters.

Disaster response: The combination of drones and satellite technology—especially during cloud coverage—can support rapid response and damage assessment efforts in an effective and timely manner, along with providing data collection and analysis.

During floods and earthquakes, drones equipped with thermal imaging cameras, noise sensing, binary sensing, and vibration sensing can help spot people in need of support or evacuation, and identify the best evacuation routes, in real-time.
Disaster recovery: Drones can support post-disaster assessments.
Satellite and drone images, combined with advanced statistical models, allow comprehensive and detailed analysis of damage and loss, especially in difficult-to-reach areas.
UAVs technology can support the development of post-disaster basemap allowing to identify critical challenges.
Disaster recovery involves rebuilding areas that were affected.
Drones can assist in the safe inspection of infrastructure so repairs can be made more effectively than with traditional inspection methods.
Created orthophotos and 3D models allow reconstructing of damaged infrastructure.
Further, drones are used to monitor the progress of aid relief and recovery efforts, including construction progress.
Such data could be used in issuing relief funds and help process insurance claims faster.

In 2017, during the catastrophic earthquake of magnitude 7.1 that hit Mexico City, more than 200 people died, 44 buildings collapsed, and almost 40% of the city lost power.

With such vast destruction, emergency response teams, NGOs, construction companies, and urban planners needed a system that would allow them to respond quickly, process large amounts of information and help develop the recovery plan.
The biggest issue during this whole process was to assess over 500 square miles of urban landscape.
DroneSky, a Mexican drone mapping company active in the construction sector, realised that with drone technology they were capable to help Mexico City to quickly inspect the damage.
From previous experience, the company knew that drone mapping, besides creating an immediate record of destruction, could also help analyse the data in a meaningful way.
Disaster response: Initially, drones helped to inspect the scale of the damage, giving a superior view compared to assessing the destruction from the ground.
Just two days after the earthquake, DroneSky had used a DJI Phantom 4 to map the entire Xochimilco district, one of the hardest hit and most marginalised areas in the city.
In eight flights, they created a map of the whole 98.6-acre neighbourhood.
Moreover, they created individual maps of specific buildings that had suffered the most damage.
Disaster recovery: DroneSky used DroneDeploy’s cloud-based drone mapping platform to create orthomosaic maps, elevation models, and 3D-point clouds that easily integrate with 3D-modelling software.
Besides sharing their maps with NGOs, urban planners, and anyone else who might benefit from them, DroneSky mobilised a group of architecture students.
Aiming to create a plan for the complete regeneration of public space in the district, students formed the Rebuilding Mexico Group.
Using the drone-generated maps and 3D surface models as a baseline, the group had intentions to redesign eight major buildings which had been destroyed.

According to the co-founders of DroneSky, this recovery project represented a new way of responding to natural disasters, not only in terms of new, innovative technology, but also new ways of thinking, reacting, and helping communities after a crisis.

Modern sustainability goals force authorities to approach urban planning and expansion with limited resources.

The aforementioned expansion of urban areas requires massive data collection for planning purposes.

Because drones can fly at very low altitudes, they can produce fine-grained images of 1 cm resolution or better, enabling the production of precise 2D orthomosaics or 3D models of streets or properties, and generating statistics on the occupation of dwellings, infrastructure, and public spaces.

With this more accurate picture of residential development, agencies and stakeholders are in a better position to transition informal settlers toward formal property ownership and participation in urban planning processes, and accelerate the process of generating an accurate cadastre system.

Provision of sufficient transport services is a major challenge for most of the LAC region, for two reasons.
First, due to the extremely high population density in major cities and the uneven distribution of the population in rural areas, it is difficult to design a dense, affordable road network.

Second, even though the region’s high urbanisation rate (80%) and relatively high income call for sophisticated urban transport systems, Latin America’s paved roads are similar in density and quality to those in Africa.
The region is characterised by a combination of large areas of inaccessibility and congestion challenges, particularly in cities and megacities.
Inadequate urban public transportation limits residents’ access to jobs, schools, and health services, hindering both productivity and equity.
In fact, the average travel time to and from work in the LAC region is 77 minutes, whereas in advanced economies it takes just 65 minutes, despite longer travel distances.
Therefore, the region’s infrastructure can be considered to be of rather low quality.
Proper transportation brings many opportunities and opens doors for competitive global trade.
Besides urban transport, the biggest need in the region is for country-wide roads, railways, and ports, to speed exports as well as transporting workers from rural areas.

Cyclical road infrastructure monitoring using drones may lead to significant optimisation of maintenance works planning, reduction of costs related to inspections, preventive maintenance, and better understanding and preparedness for resilience to natural hazards .The drone applications for road infrastructure monitoring and maintenance are multiple, including road and time-sensitive land surveys, precise mapping, maintenance and asset inspection, post-project documentation, highways infrastructure maintenance, bridge inspection, pavement condition, road distress and vulnerability to disasters analysis and monitoring.
The precision of drone images even allows the detection of different road/pavement defects, such as ruts, potholes, edge failures, ravelling, delamination, cracks, bleeding, corrugations or shoving.

The precise visual data, content, and measurements provided by drones are obtained and analysed with the aid of LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensors and Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology.
Drone data can be processed into many different deliverables (e.g. bare terrain models) for road surroundings mapping.
Drone imagery is used to create orthophotomaps that portray accuracy and detail, while the technology can also be utilised to create 3D visual representation of real assets ( digital twins ).
High resolution inspection photos can be also delivered to support remote and precise objects’ examination.
The technology for data collection in difficult to reach spots (such as bridge inspections) is fully mature.
Images and video captured by drones are subsequently viewed by human inspectors.

The adoption of a drone-based approach for inspections across the LAC region is still limited, however, technology has been validated and is already in use in countries such as Uruguay, Brazil, Argentina and to some extent in Guatemala.
Road condition monitoring is less mature as a solution, although it has been successfully used by several road agencies across the globe.
In the LAC region this use has not yet been widely validated.

Drone data can be captured and used in an organised cyclical manner in order to inspect road infrastructure towards potential damages and issues (e.g. construction cracking due to land movements), in post disaster technical shape inspections as well as during construction and re-construction works to verify results quality.
Inspections via drones are a time- and cost-saving solution, and increase the climate resilience of road infrastructure.

In 2019, the World Bank Group published the study called “Improving Climate Resilience of Federal Road Newtork in Brazil” during which drones were partially used for establishing the geohazard risk mitigation methodologies for roads.
The small drones were used as a low-cost alternative for topographic characterization, slope control and disaster prevention of the transport infrastructure.

The results obtained indicate an excellent cost-benefit ratio of the use of drones, given the low investment, fast processing time of data, and the reduction of the team required for it analysis , as well as extremely consistent results for planning, monitoring, and maintenance of road works.

The Caribbean Island of Sint Eustatius was hit by two major hurricanes, Irma and Maria, during the high-intensity season of 2017.
It caused major destruction on the island’s natural life and infrastructure, including to the local airport.
The airport’s airstrip is located at the edge of a coastal cliff, which was severely eroded during the storm.

This caused significant risk to the safety of air operations and had adverse consequences for the island’s entire population—as, in the absence of a large marine port, the airport has been the main means of transportation to and from the island for both people and cargo.
In 2018, Dutch company GeoInspect performed a drone survey and inspection of the damage to the airstrip and the structure of the cliff.
The project started by obtaining the permissions to operate a drone over the airport, which required coordination with the local authorities as well as close cooperation with the airport tower.
The project involved performing a photogrammetry survey as well as high-accuracy LiDAR scanning.
The detailed 3D point cloud allowed GeoInspect to safely map and analyse the otherwise inaccessible gullies of the cliff.

Data analysis revealed that the damage had been caused by rainwater running back down the side of the hills and flowing toward the sea, rather than heavy waves crashing against the coastline as initially presumed.

Armed with this information, a local engineering company planned to canalize the runoff, by creating a new system of culverts and canals to enable the rainwater to flow in a different direction, away from the airstrip and cliffs.
The analysis allowed key decisions to be made, preventing further erosion and damage on the infrastructure, and helping to guarantee the safety and continued operation of the airport.
Additionally, the data gathered from the survey could be used in the future as a baseline for further analysis of the erosion of the cliff.
Future survey data can be overlayed on top of the original 3D point cloud and analysed with a high level of accuracy.

According to a joint report by the Inter-American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture (IICA), the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and Microsoft, nearly 224 million people (32% of the LAC region population) have no access to the internet at the minimum necessary quality standard.

According to IDB, US$ 68.5 billion would be needed to overcome this digital gap: 59% of this amount should be used to improve connectivity in cities and 41% should go to rural areas, where public investments tend to be the main financing source.

To achieve equal access to the internet across the region, both affordable prices and high-quality infrastructure are essential.
There is a wide gap between individual LAC countries in terms of quality of service.
Chile and Uruguay are the two countries best placed in terms of connectivity—although only 15% of connections have speeds greater than 15 Mbps (megabits per second).
At the other end of the spectrum, Bolivia has one of the region's lowest connectivity rates, mainly due to experiencing the highest prices.
Remote internet access is also of vital importance to LAC countries due to the large number of natural disasters that occur in the region every year.

By providing remote internet access, this obstacle can be overcome, increasing people’s chances of survival.

In November 2016, a group of researchers used drones to find and monitor the Amazon river dolphins , also known as the pink river dolphin or boto.

Although these animals are relatively abundant, they are considered to be a highly vulnerable species due to dams that fragment and threaten certain populations, and due to other threats such as contamination of rivers and lakes.
The team surveyed river dolphins along 80km of the Juruá River, Brazil.
Two drones were deployed from a boat, travelling at a constant speed, at an altitude of around 20m, 50m from the side of the boat, monitoring a 100m stretch parallel to the river margin.
Video was continually recorded using a camera positioned at 35° to the water surface.
All of these variables were specifically chosen to achieve a drone perspective similar to a human observer.
To ensure that the impact on wildlife would be minimal, researchers followed operational protocols and best practices for drone flight operation.

A trial flight in an area with high population density enabled them to secure the number of observations necessary to assess detectability and to evaluate the possible impacts of drones on animal behaviour.
Simultaneously, three observers were looking for dolphins.
For each sighting, observers reported group size, the presence of calves, sighting angle relative to the trackline, and estimated distances from the boat and river margin.
It was discovered that on-board observers made 119 observations in total, with 76 of these confirmed by drone footage.
Researchers believe that the difference in the number of observations was the result of drone camera resolution and the distance at which the dolphins were detected.
Therefore, the use of a higher resolution camera could decrease the difference in number of observations.
Eventually, the aerial survey provided higher accuracy in counting individuals during the detection of groups.
The images captured by UAVs confirmed identifications and facilitated correlation between species and use of habitats with a high degree of precision.
The use of drones also reduced the bias caused by responsive movement.

Due to its geographical location, the LAC region is highly vulnerable to mosquito-borne disease outbursts.
Malaria, dengue fever and Zika are present with varying degrees of incidence.
Malaria is the disease that poses the biggest threat to people.

Although countries like Argentina, Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador and Paraguay have put great efforts into reducing new cases of malaria, to the point where it has been nearly or completely eradicated, there are still countries with high rates of the disease.
The biggest incidence in the region can be found in Guyana and Venezuela, with 34 and 33 cases respectively per 1,000 at-risk population in 2019.
Moreover, Venezuela also shows the largest number of estimated malaria deaths (with 456 people dying of the disease), followed by Haiti, Guyana and Brazil (with 81, 33 and 30 deaths, respectively).
Dengue also remains a public health problem in the LAC region despite the efforts of countries to stop and mitigate it.
The incidence of dengue in the region is heterogeneous, and particularly high in Nicaragua, with 934 cases per 100,000 population in 2018, followed by Belize (with 564) and Paraguay (469).
Finally, Zika disease is very high in Panama, with 66 cases per 100,000 people in 2018.
Belize, Guatemala and Bolivia follow with 33, 16 and 13 cases per 100,000 people.
These diseases create economic inequalities for affected communities, which lack adequate prevention methods and modern sanitation and infrastructure.
It should be the government's priority to ensure good quality healthcare to protect people from these transmittable infections.
Outbreak preparedness and control is crucial for a proper prevention and response, for which countries should develop their capacities and resources.
For instance, the use of insecticide-treated nets and indoor residual spraying with insecticides are important preventive measures for at-risk populations to avoid mosquito bites.

The most deadly of these, malaria, also poses a real threat to crop production, exacerbating the already serious problem of malnutrition.
It has been estimated that harvests may be up to 60% lower in malaria-prone areas , due to a poor state of health which influences overall productivity levels.
Since the beginning of the century when, in 2004, mosquito-borne diseases killed almost a million people, the world has started to combat malaria and the efforts have been bringing positive outcomes.
The widespread adoption of bed nets and indoor pesticide spraying in malaria hotspots has helped prevent mosquitoes from biting and spreading disease.
However, unfortunately mosquitoes have become resistant to insecticides.
Therefore today, technology, innovation and collective efforts are essential in controlling the spread of malaria.
So far, at least three different methods of combating mosquito-borne diseases using drones have been developed.

Although all these methods were created with a mind to a conventional approach, drones have paved the way for large-scale and cost-efficient usage. 1) Drone-assisted Sterile Insect Technique (SIT): Sterilised male mosquitoes are released by drones to mate with females.
As these do not produce any offspring, the insect population declines over time.
The technique requires the uniform release of large numbers of insects in good condition over a given area.

Drones appeared to be very labour- and time-effective for this technique. 2) Drone-assisted Larval Source Management (LCM): Drones are used to spread Aquatain, a biodegradable, non-toxic, silicone-based liquid.
When poured on a body of water such as an irrigated rice paddy, the liquid will spread across the surface where it forms a thin film.

When mosquito larvae swim to the surface to breathe, they encounter the Aquatain layer, which serves as a barrier and prevents them from breathing atmospheric oxygen; within two days all larvae die. 3) Drone-assisted Wolbachia method: In this method, drones are used to release mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia bacteria which reduces their ability to transmit dengue, chikungunya or Zika between people, helping to provide communities with long-term protection from these harmful viruses.

While the practice of using drones to assist in combating malaria is still new, and while optimal practices and workflows are still being established, there is very promising evidence that drones can play a major role in upscaling the battle against malaria.
One of the first uses of drones for this sector, not just in Latin America but also globally, comes from Brazil and Mexico and dates back to 2017.
The WeRobotics organisation modified a DJI Matrice 600 drone to integrate a sterile mosquito release mechanism.
Currently, the drone technology is mature enough from a technical point of view to perform the SIT application at large scale.

According to WHO, around 3–4 million people across the Americas were infected by the Zika virus (ZIKV) in 2017.

The RTI International, the non-profit research institute committed to improving human life conditions and well-being, self-funded a number of projects in Latin America dedicated to learning more about Zika infection.

The research recognised how critical it is to gain a greater understanding of the health effects and treatment options in order to help equip world leaders with the information needed to enact policies and practices to address the virus.

The LAC region struggles with multiple environmental issues due to climate change and human-induced stresses.
Most of them are associated with air, land or water pollution.
Air pollution is a major issue, creating serious health risks and ranking in the top three leading causes of death in the region.
Air quality has mostly declined in cities due to urban development and growing industrialisation.
Today, more than 100 million people (7% of the population) in the region live in areas susceptible to air pollution levels exceeding WHO guidelines.
When it comes to water pollution , the biggest issues lie in the poor sewer systems and extensive polluting of marine ecosystems with plastic and other human waste.
Currently, 1/3 of the LAC region water is polluted due to a lack of sewage treatment.
According to the World Water Quality Assessment, it is estimated that 25 million people in rural areas throughout the region are in contact with polluted surface water originating from urban areas.
In Brazil alone, water is of ‘poor’ or ‘terrible’ quality in 40% of rivers, creeks and lakes, leaving 77 million people without access to safe water.
Marine pollution , in the form of plastic, sewage or chemicals, poses a risk to fisheries and tourism, on which many countries’ economies depend.
Tourism accounts for 15.2% of GDP in the Caribbean, and over 50% in some countries like Grenada.
Coral reefs—of huge value for biodiversity and with great appeal for the tourism industry—are being degraded by marine litter.
The amount of plastic found on Caribbean beaches reaches 2,014 items of litter per kilometre (compared to an average of 573 worldwide).

With regard to soil pollution , in 2016 more than 68% of the soil in the LAC region was affected by erosion: 100 million ha of land have been degraded due to deforestation and 70 million have been overgrazed.
Without a long-term solution, desertification and land degradation will affect food supply, lead to increased migration, and threaten the stability of many nations and regions.
For example, in Bolivia, 77% of the population live in degraded areas.
In Argentina, Mexico and Paraguay, over 50% of the territory suffers problems linked to degradation or desertification.
Finally, in Brazil, desertification affects 18% of the territory, influencing crops such as maize and beans.
With the world facing the threat of climate change, environmental pollution monitoring is of utmost importance.
The proper assessment of environmental conditions and trends is beneficial for wildlife and a healthy environment is critical to public health and the sustainability of societies.
According to the UN, there is an increasing need to develop and implement large-scale monitoring policies that aim to counteract the current level of air, land, and water pollution.
This necessitates going beyond the current technological approach and adopting more advanced systems that guarantee continuous and pervasive environmental monitoring.
Drones are used for a variety of environmental monitoring purposes, such as assessing air, water or soil pollution, carrying different kinds of sensors and equipment.
Air pollution : the amount of aerosols and pollutants in the air varies significantly at different elevations.
Therefore, drones can bring significantly better data on air pollutants and their pattern of spread compared to ground-based sensor stations.
Equipped with dedicated gas sensors, they can be deployed to trace GHGs and other pollutants (e.g. PM2.5, PM10, CO) at different altitudes with high spatial and temporal resolution.
Based on drone data, the fine-grained air quality index (AQI) can also be mapped.

Soil pollution : drones equipped with multispectral and hyperspectral sensors generate data that, when appropriately processed, can bring information about soil contamination (usually with infrared and shortwave-infrared bands).

Water pollution : drones mounted with hyperspectral sensors can capture characteristics of water surface reflectance, and can therefore detect suspended solids, particulate matter and biological or chemical toxic agents.
Thermal sensors can detect plastic debris that are threatening aquatic wildlife such as coral reefs and species that thrive in the fragile ecosystem.

Underwater drones, when deployed within the top 9 meters of water where the majority of microplastic can be found, can help in determining where microplastics are most likely to occur, which better informs prevention strategies.
The amount of evidence of the use of drones for environmental pollution monitoring from every region in the world suggests that the adoption of the technology is at a fairly high level.
Also, in the case of marine areas, aquatic drones are becoming more and more popular.
They allow researchers to gain insights about water contamination at different depths, especially regarding microplastics.
In the LAC region, adoption of the technology also seems to be fairly widespread.

The evidence comes from countries like Peru (where drones are used to measure GHG concentration in remote areas of the Peruvian Andes and in Lima), Mexico (measuring pollutants and monitoring coral reefs), Brazil (monitoring of soil contamination and the water toxicity level in the Tiete River), Argentina (aquatic drones monitoring water pollution), and Chile (monitoring land changes like desertification).

Mexico has some particular areas that suffer from serious environmental problems.
The city of Torreón, located in the Lagunera region of Coahuila state, was ranked as the fourth highest among the 248 most contaminated regions in the world in terms of ammonia concentration.
The main sources of this contamination are the metallurgical industry, the fertilizer industry, and the dairy industry—including both livestock and forage crops.

Although ammonia is not usually considered by official standards due to its small presence in natural conditions, when combined with other acidic contaminants, such as sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx), ammonia (NH3) becomes ammonium (NH4+), which has a high diffusion range, extending several hundred kilometres (between 100 and 1000km) from its point of origin.
A group of researchers proposed a smart multi-sensor drone system to monitor air quality at the La Laguna Technological Institute monitoring site near Torreón city.
The measurements were performed at different altitudes: ground, 10m, 30m, 50m or 100m.
The multi-sensor system used to trace pollutants was placed on a support structure mounted on the drone, and the concentrations of SO2, NH3, CO, NO2, PM10, and PM2.5 were monitored.
Every 6 seconds, 168 to 250 samples were acquired.
Following data collection, the data was compared with data obtained from international air quality measurement systems.
The values provided by the proposed drone system correspond to real-time measurements at specific locations, whereas the data reports from the international databases are based on a 24-hour average.
The drone measurement system, using low-cost sensors, proved to be a very useful alternative to complement the data obtained by (or missing from) other methods of measuring air quality pollutants.
Real-time data, when acquired continuously, can help government agencies, health ministries, and policymakers to take proactive immediate, mid-, and long-term actions.

These might include preventive closure of schools or parks when the air pollution levels are extremely high, introduction of restrictions on the number of cars circulating, or temporary closure of industries that are polluting above the legal levels authorised by the authorities.
And in the mid-to-long term, it will inform the introduction of further local air quality regulations in order to prevent risks to the population in the region.

The development of the integration process developed within the framework of the ALADI aims at promoting the harmonious and balanced socio-economic development of the region, and its long-term objective is the gradual and progressive establishment of a Latin-American single market.
